It looks like OpenAI (you?) just released some work on the problems we've been thinking about. Is the work that led to the new quasi-RH work similar to the work we've been doing, or does it take a different approach?

[https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/The-Quasi-Riemann-Hypothesis-October-5-2026/paper2.pdf](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/The-Quasi-Riemann-Hypothesis-October-5-2026/paper2.pdf)
I’ll read the new paper and compare its main argument with our shifted-zeta positivity work. I’ll focus on the mathematical overlap and where the approaches differ.

I’m using the PDF reading workflow to check the paper’s statements and proof structure. I’ll also compare it with our recent prime-variance work, since that may be closer to this result than the earlier positivity approaches.

The closest connection is to our recent prime-variance program: both seek a fixed power saving that would exclude zeros from a fixed strip near \(\Re s=1\). The new paper’s mechanism is different, though—it uses families of Möbius sums, cubic theta functions, and large-sieve estimates. I’m checking what its claimed bound would imply for our variance exponent.

The exponent conversion is clear: their \(11/12\) bound would give \(\delta=5/6\) in our framework, meeting our first fixed-saving milestone if the theorem holds. The release also lists a stronger \(7/8\) companion result, corresponding to \(\delta=3/4\).

Their iteration reduces the scales of auxiliary sums; it does not repeatedly improve the zero-free boundary toward RH. I’m saving that distinction and the comparison in our investigation’s notes, using the write-page skill and your repository’s format.

**The goal is very close to our recent work; the mechanism is substantially different.** The strongest connection is to our October 3–4 prime-variance and Möbius-cancellation investigations, rather than the earlier Weil-positivity, Sonin, or physical-realization approaches.

On “you?”: OpenAI attributes this release to an **unreleased internal model**, with human editing of the \(11/12\) paper. I can’t identify that model with this chat. [Release description](https://github.com/openai/math#how-the-results-were-produced).

Our recent program established the correspondence
\[
\mathcal V_g(X)=O(X^{2+\delta})
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
|\Re\rho-\tfrac12|\le \tfrac{\delta}{2}.
\]
We then sought the missing arithmetic input: **any fixed global power saving**, meaning some \(\delta<1\). Our reductions preserve the signed Möbius/Vaughan contributions, but have not supplied that saving. See :codex-file-citation{path="/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/prime-variance-exponents/manuscript.tex" purpose="source"}.

The new paper approaches this through a specially constructed **family of arithmetic sums**:

1. It embeds a Möbius sum into a family of sextic-character twists over the Eisenstein integers.
2. At parameters \(u=p^6\), many family members reproduce the original sum, apart from controlled errors. A sufficiently strong average bound therefore controls that particular sum.
3. Poisson summation converts Möbius coefficients into cubic Gauss sums. A cubic theta transformation then produces quadratic characters, permitting a stronger large-sieve estimate.
4. Möbius inversion and a recursive transfer control the additional cube terms introduced along the way.

That family amplification is the distinctive idea. Their recursion reduces **auxiliary scales**; it does not repeatedly improve the zero-free boundary toward \(1/2\). These mechanisms appear in §2, with the nonvanishing deduction in §3 of :codex-file-citation{path="/tmp/quasi-rh-comparison/paper2.pdf" purpose="source"}.

There is a particularly interesting connection to our large-values scout. We had identified that **one large detector value is insufficient** to contradict an average or density bound; some additional amplification was needed. Their character family supplies an arithmetic way to repeat a target sum many times. It is a useful counterpart to that missing idea, although it does not directly establish the amplification lemma for our existing detector. See :codex-file-citation{path="/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/prime-variance-exponents/notes/programs/09_large_values_zero_detection/PRELIMINARY_INVESTIGATION_20261004.md" purpose="source"}.

**The practical consequence for our program is concrete.** Combining the announced zero-free regions with our equivalence gives:

| External result | Our \(\delta\) | Our resulting variance bound |
|---|---:|---:|
| Linked paper: \(\Re s>11/12\) | \(5/6\) | \(O(X^{17/6})\) |
| Stronger companion: \(\Re s>7/8\) | \(3/4\) | \(O(X^{11/4})\) |
| RH endpoint | \(0\) | \(O(X^2)\) |

The release lists the \(7/8\) companion and associated formalization scope. [Catalogue](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/CONTENTS.md), [formalization description](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/lean/docs/003.md).

Thus, **if the announced theorems hold, they supply our first fixed-saving milestone through an external route**. Our next question would become how to improve that baseline—and whether their character-family structure can help control our signed covariance. They do not yet provide the exponent descent to RH that we wanted.

This is a comparison of the arguments, not an independent verification of the new proof or its Lean artifacts. I saved the detailed comparison and exponent conversion in the [investigation notes](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/prime-variance-exponents/notes/OPENAI_QUASI_RH_COMPARISON_20261008.md).
Please continue with the next question

I’ll investigate whether their character-family method can improve our new variance baseline or help control our signed covariance. I’ll first read the stronger \(7/8\) argument, then look for a concrete estimate we could transfer.
By the way, please create a new folder for this investigation with a title of your choosing within the base papers folder

I’ll put this investigation in `papers/quasi-rh-character-amplification`, with separate notes, reviews, and numerics folders. I’ll move the comparison note there and keep its links back to the prime-variance work.

I found a precise obstruction and a useful target. Feeding the \(7/8\) bound into our existing separate estimates recovers the same exponent; it gives no automatic improvement. A stronger estimate for a shorter sextic-character family could improve it, but the published theorem does not cover that range.

There may also be room for a small improvement within the companion paper’s parameter choices. I’m checking whether the apparent slack survives all its hypotheses.

The parameter lead is promising: the endpoint inequality has enough slack for a tiny shift below \(7/8\). We also found that several lemmas are explicitly restricted to \(7/8\), so substitution alone would be invalid. Their displayed local bounds appear to extend to the needed region; I’m having that extension checked independently before recording its status.

The written derivation passed the targeted internal review and exact arithmetic checks. Conditional on the companion paper’s structural lemmas, it supports the tiny change
\[
\frac78\;\longrightarrow\;\frac78-\frac1{600000}.
\]
I’m recording it as a conditional extension for further review. The larger question—whether shorter character families can produce a substantial gain—still needs a new estimate.

Created **[Quasi-RH Character Amplification](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/quasi-rh-character-amplification/README.md)** under the base `papers` folder and moved the comparison there.

Continuing the investigation produced a **small conditional extension** of the stronger companion paper’s argument:
\[
\Re s>\frac78-\frac1{600000}.
\]
In our variance framework, this corresponds to
\[
\mathcal V_g(X)=O\!\left(X^{\,11/4-1/300000}\right).
\]

The proposed gain comes from adjusting the parameters while retaining a saving that the published estimates discard. The derivation also addresses the contour domains affected by that adjustment. Exact arithmetic checks and separate reviews by agents using the same model passed. **Its status remains conditional on the paper’s structural lemmas**; I have not independently audited the full external proof or replayed Lean.

Saved:
- [Derivation and assumptions](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/quasi-rh-character-amplification/notes/PARAMETER_EXTENSION_20261008.md)
- [Scoped review](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/quasi-rh-character-amplification/reviews/PARAMETER_EXTENSION_REVIEW_20261008.md)
- [Character-family transfer analysis](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/quasi-rh-character-amplification/notes/CHARACTER_FAMILY_TRANSFER_20261008.md)

For a substantial improvement, the concrete missing ingredient is a mean-square estimate for **shorter character families**. Our current signed-covariance estimates do not supply that gain automatically. The next priority is auditing the imported lemmas before optimizing further.
Please continue with the improvements
I’ll audit the lemmas behind the proposed gain, then check whether the parameters allow a stronger improvement. I’ll save the derivation and review in the new investigation folder.

The low-estimate audit supports the proposed adjustment: the saving survives over a much wider parameter range than we used. The tighter constraint appears to be the count of exceptional character rows. I’m checking that bound over the full range of parameters with exact arithmetic.

There’s a useful additional adjustment: the total length of the prime slots can vary while the low estimate keeps the same form. Together with a sharper exact bound for exceptional rows, this appears to give about 25 times the previous gain. I’m checking the remaining parameter ranges and contour estimates before recording that result.

The exact certificate now supports the conditional boundary
\[
\frac78-\frac1{24000}\approx0.87495833.
\]
That is 25 times the previous gain, though the absolute change is still small. I also found where this parameter choice stops working, so it cannot simply be repeated toward RH. The derivation and scoped audits are being saved now.

I strengthened the **conditional candidate** to
\[
\Re s>\frac78-\frac1{24000}\approx0.87495833,
\]
a **25-fold increase in the previous gain**, though still small absolutely. Its variance consequence would be
\[
\mathcal V_g(X)=O\!\left(X^{11/4-1/12000}\right).
\]

The improvement changes the total prime-slot length while preserving the principal signal exponent. An exact polynomial certificate covers the full parameter range; separate scoped audits checked the low estimate, moment requirements, and contour arguments.

**The result remains conditional on the external structural lemmas and seven-eighths theorem.** Those deep proofs have not been independently verified here.

I also identified where this parameter family stops working—near boundary \(0.87495720\). Further progress requires changing the geometry or strengthening the exceptional-row estimate.

Saved the [full derivation](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/quasi-rh-character-amplification/notes/GEOMETRY_OPTIMIZATION_20261008.md), with three reviews and reproducible exact checks linked from the [investigation guide](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/quasi-rh-character-amplification/README.md).
What are some ideas for changing the geometry or strengthening the exceptional-row estimates? Does anything from the repo give you ideas for this?
I’ll check which geometric constraints are actually binding, then look through the repo for techniques that could improve the exceptional-row count or change how it enters the argument.

The repo points to a concrete possibility: use more of the relationship between the inverse and plain witnesses on the same row. The source already combines each witness with prime-slot information, but then compares the resulting bounds separately. Our covariance and Schur-complement work suggests testing what a mixed estimate could retain. I also checked the unused scale parameter; adjusting it alone appears to offer only a small further gain.

I’d prioritize a mixed witness estimate for the nearly saturated bad rows, with a second track comparing probes that share the same principal signal. The repo gives useful identities and examples showing why cross terms matter, but neither route has the needed power-saving estimate yet. I’m saving a ranked research note with those targets and their limitations.

Yes. **The repo’s strongest clue is to preserve correlations that disappear when we estimate components separately.** It offers concrete ways to investigate that, although it does not yet supply the missing exceptional-row bound.

I would prioritize these directions:

1. **Estimate the inverse and plain witnesses jointly.**

   The troublesome rows produce large inverse and plain Dirichlet polynomials for the **same character and height**. The source already combines each witness with prime slots, but its final comparison uses the better of two separate moment bounds. A mixed estimate could exploit their additional dependence. [Companion paper](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/The-Quasi-Riemann-Hypothesis-September-30-2026/paper.pdf)

   This closely matches our [arithmetic-overlap result](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/prime-variance-exponents/notes/programs/01_signed_arithmetic_covariance/ARITHMETIC_OVERLAP_20261004.md): an actual semiprime contribution is too large by itself, making its cross term with the cofactor contribution essential.

   The target can be narrow: improve the exceptional-row exponent near \(\delta\approx0.38669\), where the current estimate is tight. A saving \(R^*\mapsto R^*-\eta\) improves the high exponent by exactly \(h\eta\). We would need a new mixed-moment argument; multiplying the existing bounds does not establish independence.

2. **Combine probes that share the same principal signal.**

   Construct two or three admissible probes with different slot windows or scales, normalize them to the same signal, and retain their mixed error terms. Differences between those probes then have zero principal signal and might cancel part of the exceptional contribution.

   Our [source-selective Schur analysis](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations/sonin-critical-boundary/notes/selective-loss-program/01_schur_completion_20261003.md) suggests the precise quantity to examine:
   \[
   G_{00}-G_{0C}G_{CC}^{-1}G_{C0},
   \]
   the residual error energy after using the contrasts.

   The first experiment should derive the mixed leading kernel near the bad bin. We need an exact cancellation or a **power saving**; a constant improvement in this matrix changes no exponent. The coefficients must also be explicitly controlled.

3. **Test geometry beyond \(M+\ell=1\), with the full low-estimate cost retained.**

   Our successful adjustment preserves that equality. Allowing \(M+\ell>1\) could improve the high side, but it breaks the comparison that keeps the dual row range within the physical row range.

   This is a concrete calculation to attempt: return to the unspecialized low-energy estimate, retain its full maximum, and determine whether the additional cost outweighs the high-side benefit. The repo’s complete-response work is useful guidance here: omitted boundary and support terms can manufacture an apparent gain.

   Merely optimizing the remaining parameter \(b\) appears less promising. Exploratory calculations suggest only about \(1.3\times10^{-7}\) additional boundary gain beyond our present parameter-family limit.

4. **Strengthen the long-witness estimate through shorter character families.**

   The existing unmarked mean square requires more rows than polynomial length. Even a modest extension below that threshold would improve the competing long-witness branch.

   This is the precise open input identified in our [character-family transfer note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/quasi-rh-character-amplification/notes/CHARACTER_FAMILY_TRANSFER_20261008.md). It has greater potential, but requires substantial new arithmetic. The restriction to actual Möbius coefficients is essential.

**My first choice is the joint-witness route**, preceded by keeping the full prime-amplitude profile to isolate the nearly saturated rows. In parallel, I would test two common-signal probes using the Schur approach.

I saved the detailed targets, limitations, and sensitivity calculations in the [research directions note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/quasi-rh-character-amplification/notes/RESEARCH_DIRECTIONS_20261008.md).
Excellent, please continue in the order you proposed

I’ll first retain the full prime-amplitude profile and identify which rows still make the bound tight. Then I’ll examine the joint inverse/plain witnesses on that class. In parallel, I’ll check whether two admissible probes can share the same principal signal and yield a useful mixed error estimate.

The profile calculation exposes a useful distinction: uneven prime-slot amplitudes can improve the existing bounds after the witness cutoff is retuned, but the hardest nearly saturated profiles remain. I’m narrowing the unresolved estimate to that class and calculating how much additional saving would be sufficient for a specific next boundary.

The profile refinement now isolates the unresolved rows quite sharply: their amplitudes are nearly saturated, and retuning the witness cutoff gives them little benefit. The two other routes also have clearer limits: two probes can cancel one known mode, while off-balance geometry pays an explicit cost. I’m checking and saving the precise mixed-moment estimate that would move the next boundary.

The payoff calculation is now explicit: a uniform \(U^{-1/5000}\) saving in the mixed inverse/plain moment would suffice for the next target, \(7/8-1/20000\), after retuning both parts of the count. That saving is still unproved. The existing moments do eliminate a substantial class of uneven amplitude profiles, but leave the nearly saturated class unresolved.

The independent checks passed, including the continuous rational certificate and both cutoff adjustments. I’m saving the derivations, review, and reproducible checks in the investigation folder. The overview will keep \(7/8-1/24000\) as the current conditional candidate and mark \(7/8-1/20000\) as requiring the new mixed-moment estimate.

Continued in the proposed order. The main progress is a sharper, quantitative description of the remaining obstacle.

1. **Full amplitude profiles help.** Using the existing assumed moment estimates, I derived a stronger count and retuned the detector cutoff. The remaining difficult rows are nearly saturated: at least 80% of their prime-slot length has amplitude at least 90% of the maximum. Perfect saturation survives this refinement.

2. **The joint-witness target is now precise.** A uniform \(U^{-1/5000}\) saving in the mixed moment
   \[
   \sum_{\mathcal C}|M_rS_mQ_I|^2
   \]
   on that restricted class would suffice for the next boundary \(7/8-1/20000\), after both necessary rebalances. **That mixed estimate remains unproved**, so the current conditional candidate stays \(7/8-1/24000\).

3. **Two common-signal probes:** I constructed explicit probes and their exact mixed error kernel. They can cancel one prescribed mode, but a uniform power saving still requires new arithmetic information.

4. **Off-balance geometry:** retaining the dual-length cost raises the low-side boundary by \(7\tau/12\) near our current geometry. It therefore offers no immediate improvement with the existing estimates.

The exact rational checks and separate scoped review passed. Everything is saved in the investigation folder: [full synthesis and next estimate](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/quasi-rh-character-amplification/notes/LOCALIZED_JOINT_WITNESS_TARGET_20261008.md).
Please continue with the first remaining task
I’ll expand the restricted mixed moment with the actual inverse, plain, and prime-slot coefficients, then look for a specific term where the required saving could come from.

The expansion has produced a useful bound: column pairs with small ratio-character conductor already fit comfortably within the required estimate. This includes the ordinary diagonal and all sixth-power coincidences. I’m combining that bound with the existing row count to isolate the large-conductor pairs that still need cancellation.

Two useful restrictions now follow from the existing inputs. The new estimate is only needed for rows with primitive conductor above \(U^{2m-0.001}\), and—within those rows—for distinct plain-factor ideals whose ratio conductor exceeds \(U^{4/5}\). The discarded terms have explicit positive margins. I’m checking how this remaining signed sum fits the source’s transformed moment argument.

The transfer check found why the existing inverse-moment proof does not close this last step: adding the plain factor both enlarges the transformed row range beyond its allowed widths and leaves a divisor coefficient that the source theorem excludes. I’ve kept those obstructions separate from the new bounds, so the notes distinguish what we have removed from what remains unproved.

The combined reduction passed a separate review. All discarded contributions are below the target mixed-moment exponent by at least \(1/6250\), before adjustable losses. I’m saving the exact remaining signed sum, the three reduction proofs, and the arithmetic checks; the estimate for that final sum is still open.

The expansion yielded **three useful partial bounds**, under the same imported source assumptions:

- Rows with primitive conductor \(Q_\psi\le U^{2m-1/1000}\) already satisfy the required mixed saving.
- The entire plain-factor diagonal \(k=k'\) contributes only \(O(U^{1+\epsilon})\).
- Column pairs whose ratio-character conductor is at most \(U^{4/5}\) are controlled by an elementary ideal-pair count.

Together, these reduce the moment to **one explicit signed sum** over distinct plain ideals, large-conductor rows, and large-conductor column ratios. All discarded contributions lie below the target exponent by at least \(1/6250\), before adjustable losses.

I also checked the proposed transfer of the source’s inverse-moment proof. It fails at two concrete points: the transformed row range becomes too long, and the transformed divisor coefficient falls outside the theorem’s allowed class.

The remaining signed estimate is still unproved, so the current conditional boundary is unchanged. The separate review and exact arithmetic checks passed.

Saved the [combined derivation and precise remaining sum](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/quasi-rh-character-amplification/notes/MIXED_MOMENT_REDUCTION_20261008.md), with linked proofs, review, and reproducible checks.
Please write this into a draft manuscript

I’ll turn the reductions into a manuscript that states the proved conditional results, the exact remaining estimate, and the limits of the source transfer. I’ll include the author attribution and LLM acknowledgement, then compile it in the built-in LaTeX editor.

I’m making the main theorem self-contained: it will state the three analytic inputs explicitly, then prove the reduction to one signed sum. The possible improvement to \(7/8-1/20000\) will appear separately as a conditional application, since the remaining estimate has not been proved.

The draft compiles successfully. The reviews found a few precision edits: making the remaining estimate explicitly one-sided, stating the prime-slot supply condition, and distinguishing exact gains from gains after rounding losses. I’m incorporating those and adding the manuscript history entry.

Created the [draft manuscript](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/quasi-rh-character-amplification/manuscript.tex), including proofs, explicit assumptions, conditional payoff, author attribution, and an LLM acknowledgement.

It compiles successfully. The remaining signed estimate is clearly marked as open. I also saved the mathematical review and added the concise manuscript history entry.

## My request:
Excellent, what are the next steps for this project?
I’ll check the manuscript’s remaining estimate and the investigation notes, then lay out the next steps in priority order.

The next priority is **finding cancellation in the remaining signed sum**. We now know which contributions are harmless and exactly where the existing proof stops.

I recommend this order:

1. **Track the plain divisor through the transformed sum.**  
   In the remaining coefficient \(h(tfn)\), split the plain ideal as
   \[
   k=k_0k_1,\qquad k_0\mid tf,\quad k_1\mid n.
   \]
   Keep \(k_1\) as a summation variable, preserving its Möbius signs. Recalculate the actual lengths, conductors, and masks in each size range. This tests whether a bilinear estimate can recover cancellation lost by treating \(h\) as an arbitrary coefficient. The critical case is when almost all the plain factor remains inside \(n\).

2. **Resolve how to retain the exceptional-row restriction.**  
   Compare a direct estimate on the selected rows with a bound for a larger, positive smooth-family moment. Before investing in the latter, test its strength on principal-character and sixth-power rows: enlarging the family may demand substantially more than our original target. This decision determines which transformations are legitimate.

3. **Prove a saving in a precisely defined surviving case.**  
   Start with the squarefree, coprime case and fixed profiles. A useful first result would be a positive power saving with an explicit range of validity. Then extend it to overlaps, prime powers, the full length rectangle, and the required height derivatives. Ultimately, the application needs the \(1/5000\) mixed-moment saving uniformly—not just at the numerical bottleneck.

4. **Run an independent validation track alongside the research.**  
   Seek specialist review of the elementary pair-count lemma and the exact imported analytic inputs. Preserve the reviewed manuscript as a Git milestone, with subsequent results linked through the history file.

**The immediate next calculation should be step 1, accompanied by the feasibility check in step 2.** Its success criterion is concrete: either the retained divisor structure produces a usable saving, or we identify the specific surviving range that requires a genuinely new estimate.
Excellent, please write this into a continuation note, and suggest whether to use Codex or ChatGPT

I’ll save the ordered plan as a continuation note and link it from the investigation overview. I’ll also check the current product guidance before recommending how to divide the next work between Codex and ChatGPT.

I’m using OpenAI Docs for the product comparison. I’m also making the row-selector check an explicit first gate in the note: enlarging the family introduces principal-character rows that may require estimates we do not yet have. That should be settled before investing in the transformed divisor argument.

The note will preserve the exact open estimate, the failed shortcuts, and concrete completion criteria for each next step. I recommend continuing in Codex for the repository work, with a fresh ChatGPT session for a focused critique. The current documentation describes substantial overlap between them, so this is a workflow recommendation, not a ranking of mathematical ability.

The continuation note is ready, including a prompt for the next session. Its first task has three possible outcomes: the extra rows are controlled, a specific new estimate is needed, or the profiles leave the test inconclusive. This keeps a limitation of our current estimates from being mistaken for a counterexample.

Saved the [continuation note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/quasi-rh-character-amplification/notes/CONTINUATION_20261008.md) and linked it from the investigation overview. It includes the ordered tasks, exact open estimate, completion criteria, and a next-session prompt.
